subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OPERATION OF FLYING SCHOOLS, PRODUCTION OF AIRCRAFT, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO OPERATION OF FLYING SCHOOLS, PRODUCTION OF AIRCRAFT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will
recall that, in the statement I made on February 5, I said that the government had offered to the North Atlantic treaty organization to train additional aircrew. The number proposed was 1,100 per annum, which would bring the total to be trained for NATO and the United Kingdom something over 1,300 per annum.
We have now received the recommendation of the standing group that all the places available in respect of this additional number up to December 31 of this year should be allocated to the United Kingdom. After that the allocation will be reconsidered.
At present our plans provide for a build-up to an annual output of aircrew of over 3,000. That represents an increase of six times the figure for 1950 and fifteen times the figure for the previous year.
This will be accompanied by a fivefold increase in groundcrew training facilities.
Administrative establishments will also be increased though not to the same extent.
This will require the reopening of a number of airfields. During the war we had a total of 56 airfields used for training either under the British commonwealth air training plan or other plans.
Air Training Plan
We already have air training schools and operational stations or other units in operation or under construction at Goose Bay, and, to a very limited extent, Torbay in Newfoundland; at Summerside in Prince Edward Island; at Dartmouth and Greenwood in Nova Scotia; at Moncton, to a limited extent, and Chatham in New Brunswick; at Bagotville, St. Hubert, St. Johns and Dorval in Quebec; at Rockcliffe, Uplands, Arnprior, Trenton, Downsview, North Bay, Centralia, Clinton and Aylmer in Ontario; at Winnipeg, Gimli and Rivers in Manitoba; at Edmonton, Calgary and Suffield in Alberta; and at Patricia Bay, again to a limited extent, and Vancouver in British Columbia. There are, of course, other headquarters and depots in addition.
Experience during the second world war, when Canada trained 131,000 aircrew, showed that the best places for flying training was in the prairie provinces. Located in these provinces are a number of flying fields with runways, hangars and buildings in a relatively good state of repair, enabling re-establishment to be done as speedily and economically as possible.
Accordingly, all the new flying schools will be located in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Also, to facilitate maintenance and administration and to take advantage of more suitable weather, basic flying training schools will be grouped in the western part of this area, while advanced flying schools will be grouped in the eastern part of this area.
The new schools to be re-established are flying training schools at Claresholm and Penhold in Alberta and Moose Jaw in Saskatchewan. Advanced flying training schools are to be at Saskatoon in Saskatchewan and Portage la Prairie in Manitoba, with a gunnery school at Macdonald. The flying training school at Gimli will later be converted to an advanced training school. A large air navigation school will be established at Winnipeg in addition to the present school at Summer-side, P.E.I.
Of the existing establishments, Aylmer, Camp Borden and Clinton in Ontario will concentrate on trades training. Selection and manning will be carried on at St. Johns, Quebec, where there will be a very large establishment.
With hardly an exception, all the other establishments will be increased in accordance with the expansion of the program. Abbotsford will be used this summer for training some of the auxiliary squadrons, others going to other schools. In all probability Abbotsford will later be used as an operational station.

Air Training Plan
In this connection I should like to say that a large number of representations have been received from members of parliament, mayors, boards of trade and other representatives of most of the localities mentioned and many others. They have all offered the closest possible co-operation and reception to the R.C.A.F., with which they had such excellent relations during the war. That co-operative spirit is very greatly appreciated.
The places chosen have been selected having sole regard to two factors: first, suitability for the purpose intended; second, the condition of the existing facilities so as to provide for the most economic and speedy rehabilitation.
The facilities of all the stations will be used to the fullest extent possible. For example, by improved training methods we expect to have pupil populations of 300 at the flying training schools, as compared with 240 during the second world war. The limiting factor at each school will be the number of hours of flying that physically can be fitted in, having regard to the weather and capacity of the airfield.
To operate the plan will require a large number of additional aircraft for training. My colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), announced in the house on March 5 that we would be manufacturing Harvards of the most modern type, as well as engines. In addition to meeting our own requirements, we expect to make a number of these aircraft for sale to the United States. In the meantime, our own needs can be met out of our own stocks, supplemented, if necessary, by aircraft borrowed from the United States, to be replaced out of our own production later.
We shall also be acquiring from the United States some two-seater jet training aircraft to be used until our own production enables us to meet all our own needs for this type of aircraft.
The record made during the second world war in the British commonwealth air training plan has shown that Canada is particularly qualified to make this important contribution to our collective security.

QUESTION AS TO REARRANGEMENT OF HOURS OF SITTING
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. In some sections of the press this morning there was an indication that yesterday I had made a plea in the house for shorter hours of sitting of the House of Commons. I am quite sure that the fault with the announcement in that form could not properly be laid at the doorstep of the press, but was rather attributable to the way in which I phrased it yesterday. Perhaps I did not make my point as clear as I should have. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that what I had in mind, as I believe most members knew, was not a request for shorter sitting hours. I was only asking for a rearrangement of the present sitting hours so that they would be more convenient for members, particularly with respect to the late hours that we sit at night.
While I am on my feet, may I say how pleased I was to have had an offer of co-operation from the Prime Minister in connection with this matter. I hope that after the Easter recess we shall somehow be able to work out something which will be satisfactory to all members, and which at the same time will not interfere with the work of the house but will rather expedite it.

This we have done in order to put ourselves in a position to deal with this matter promptly as soon as we hear from Premier Campbell and give consideration to Premier Douglas' letter.
While I am on my feet, I should like to deal with a point which was raised by the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on Monday last when this same question was mentioned.
The hon. member at that time stated that both Premier Campbell and Premier Douglas had answered favourably long ago. That, Mr. Speaker, is not correct. It is true that in reply to previous letters they had both written that they favoured the proposed old age pensions amendment, in principle. The points with which we are dealing here are whether there shall be a constitutional amendment authorizing federal old age pensions, and also with the form of that amendment; and also, of course, with the substance and form of an amendment relating to a three per cent provincial indirect retail sales tax. In this connection we are dealing not with only two provinces, but with ten.

In my letter of February 28 I was chiefly concerned with observations which a number of the provincial premiers had made with respect to both the form and the substance of these two draft amendments which the federal government had previously submitted to them. Four provincial premiers had objected to the form of the old age pensions amendment. In my letter of February 28, concerning which these questions have been asked, I did submit two new alternative drafts to take care of the objections which these four provincial premiers had raised, and also of course dealt with other matters.
The replies which we have been awaiting are as to whether Premier Douglas and Premier Campbell concur in our attempts to meet the views of these other provinces. Since we wish, if at all possible, to get unanimous agreement in this matter, there is no purpose in my writing another letter to all the provincial premiers, in a further attempt to secure agreement both as to substance and as to form, until I hear from all the provincial premiers in reply to my letter of February 28. Or, to put it another way, there is no purpose in commencing another stage of the work until we complete the present stage, and we cannot complete the present stage until we hear from all the provinces concerning it.

I should like to thank the hon. member for Eglinton for having given me notice of his question.
On February 14 last the hon. member asked me whether I could indicate to the house when I expected to receive the report of the committee, and I replied then that I would think that the target date, about March 1, which was planned, would still remain the target date and that we should then shortly know whether it would be possible for us to achieve that goal in actual fact. I have since received from the Hon. Mr. Justice McQuarrie, the chairman of the committee, the reasons why this goal has not been achieved. I think that I should preface these reasons with a brief statement of the events down to the present in order that the house will understand that the committee is proceeding with the utmost haste that is compatible with the seriousness of its task.
On June 27, 1950, I announced in this house the appointment of the committee and its terms of reference.
The committee held its first meeting in Ottawa early in July, 1950. Following this meeting, the committee, in order to obtain as wide an expression of opinion as possible, notified the public, by letters to trade, labour and consumer organizations and to business firms and to the press, that for its assistance in this study the committee was anxious to receive at an early date from such organizations, firms and individuals, whatever views they might wish to express upon matters within its terms of reference.
In response to this request a considerable number of formal briefs and numerous informal letters and communications were received by the committee. There were many

Old Age Pensions
requests for delay from persons and organizations who wished to make representations but were unable, by reason of its being the summer holiday season or for other reasons, to prepare their material within the time indicated by the committee. There were also many requests for interviews. In the result, few briefs were received before mid-autumn, and briefs have continued to come in to the committee until December, 1950, the last one being received from a large national organization in a covering letter dated December 7, 1950. Many interviews were held throughout this period, that is, from midsummer to February.
The committee, since its first meeting in Ottawa on July 4, has held a considerable number of further committee meetings in Ottawa and completed a session of two and a half weeks during February, 1951. Towards the end of this last session the chairman informed me that, because of the voluminous data to be examined and the complexity of the problems that required extended study and consideration, the original target date would have to be advanced, since the work of the committee would require considerable further time before completion.
He said that he and his colleagues would do their best to finish and present their report before the end of the present session of parliament, but he could not guarantee that this would be possible.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I should like to take this opportunity to comment briefly upon the remarks made a moment ago by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). I wish to thank him for the answer he gave indicating that an endeavour is being made to reach an agreement with the various provinces as to the wording of appropriate constitutional amendments so as to make possible implementation of the old age pensions program recommended to parliament last June.
What I wish to say resolves itself into two items. In the first place I feel it would be only fair, since the Minister of Justice has referred to the fact that he received a communication from the premier of Saskatchewan today, to indicate that I have in my hand a copy of the Votes and Proceedings of the Saskatchewan legislature for Friday, March 16. From exchanges of telegrams I have had this week with the premier of Saskatchewan I believe I can say that a copy of this issue of Saskatchewan's Votes and Proceedings has been furnished to the Minister of Justice, with the letter he received this afternoon.
I note that on Friday, March 16, the Saskatchewan legislative assembly adopted two resolutions dealing with this matter, both of which were moved by Premier Douglas and seconded by Mr. Fines, the provincial treasurer. The first one deals with an amendment to the British North America Act with respect to old age pensions. The second one deals with an amendment to that same statute regarding indirect taxation within the province. May I read the first of these resolutions:
That this assembly approves in principle the amendment to the British North America Act proposed by the government of Canada following the federal-provincial conference held in December, 1950, designed to provide that while the legislature may make laws in relation to old age pensions within the province, the parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions in Canada, and authorizes the lieutenant governor in council to approve any amendment incorporating such principle or to approve any amended wording suggested by the government of Canada and deemed to embody such principle.
I will not take the time to read the other resolution. It is longer, but it concludes with the same language, namely, that the assembly has authorized the lieutenant governor in council to approve the amendment suggested in the resolution regarding indirect taxation, or any amended wording suggested by the government of Canada having the same effect. The point I wish to make clear is that in addition to the earlier stand taken by Premier Douglas in support of the general plan for the new old age pension set-up, which is what I was referring to on Monday, that province has now made clear that it is prepared to co-operate fully in the wording or the redrafting of any necessary amendments which are required so as to proceed with this matter. I hope the Minister of Justice will soon receive a similarly favourable communication from his successor in the premiership of Manitoba, Mr. Campbell,

and then he will have had communications from all ten provinces.
The other point I wish to make is that I hope the Minister of Justice and the government as a whole will proceed with this matter just as rapidly as they can. I realize the kind of difficulty that they are working under. They are dealing with constitutional amendments; they are dealing with ten provincial premiers and with the constitutional lawyers who sit at the elbows of these various premiers. Nevertheless the reason I am bringing it up is that in the speech from the throne on January 30 it was indicated that the new old age pension proposals had been laid before the provinces, and I quote:
The provincial governments are at present giving consideration to these proposals and to proposals for constitutional amendments which may require to be submitted to you before the close of the present session.
On February 5 I directed a question to the Prime Minister as to what efforts would be made by the government to deal with this matter in sufficient time so as to bring before the house at this session both the necessary amendments to the constitution and legislation based on those amendments. My latter reference was to legislation implementing the plan recommended last year by the special committee. The answer of the Prime Minister, as recorded on page 72 of Hansard, was- and I think I am fair to him if I quote the second paragraph only, since it is the relevant one:
As stated in the speech from the throne, the matter is before the provincial governments for their consideration, and it is and will be the policy of the government to avoid any possible delay when agreement has been reached to have that agreement implemented.
Those were the words of the Prime Minister. Let me point out that two or three times since then, when questions have been raised regarding early implementation of this plan, reference has been made back to that statement given by the Prime Minister on February 5. We are all agreed. We want to see action at this session. Whatever the date of the end of the session may prove to be, time is moving on; and my reason for rising at this time is to urge the government to give the best attention that they can to this matter, in the hope that their own desire, which we support very strongly, to take action at this session will be implemented before prorogation date overtakes us.

speechtext:
When this subject was being discussed yesterday the Minister of Agriculture put forward certain arguments in regard to the payment of the $65 million, which, on careful examination of Hansard, are just as impossible to understand as they were when he made the speech in the house yesterday.
The fact is that his attempt to create the impression that the $65 million was arrived at in some orderly mathematical manner is not borne out by the statement of the Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister made it quite clear that this was not a figure arrived at in that way. On March 15, as reported at page 1283 of Hansard the Prime Minister had this to say:
Now, why $65 million? From the start it had been clearly understood there could not be any mathematical calculation of the consequence of this "have regard to" clause.
Then later in his remarks the Prime Minister said:
That has been the position from the start, that there could not be any mathematical calculation of something expressed in the terms used in this agreement.
The Prime Minister then went on to say that $65 million remained of the loan of $1,250 million, and the words he used were these:
Had the government of the United Kingdom seen fit to draw that amount of $65 million and use it

as a settlement of anything legitimately or properly expected under the "have regard to" clause, the government of Canada would not have felt required to do anything more, and would have been quite content to say that everything that could reasonably be expected as a consequence of the "have regard to" clause had been discharged by that payment.
I submit that those words are not open to any misunderstanding or misinterpretation. They make it perfectly clear that in the mind of the Prime Minister the only way in which the figure of $65 million was arrived at was that there was a balance of this loan still there, and that if the suggestion of the Canadian government had been accepted and the $65 million had been taken up by the British government and then paid as the balance owing under the contract, that figure would have been accepted by the Canadian government and paid over to the pool as the amount that they were able to obtain from the government of the United Kingdom.
I mentioned the statement of the Prime Minister for this reason. He has stated clearly what actually happened. When discussion of this subject was renewed' last December and a few weeks later when the Minister of Agriculture went to England, it related- to the figure of $65 million which was the balance outstanding, just as the $100 million which was mentioned earlier related to the fact that at that time there was $115 million still outstanding. It had been reduced to $65 million, and that was the amount still there. If the government of the United Kingdom had been prepared to take that up and go through the motions of paying it over as the balance, the Canadian government was prepared to accept it.
Having said that, I then point out that we are not simply in the position that the government of the United- Kingdom has stated that it is not prepared to pay any more; we are in the position that the government that is asking that this item be approved declared by its own formal communication on May 30 of last year that it agreed that the government of the United Kingdom had fully discharged all obligations under that contract. That being so, there are no obligations remaining under the contract. I come back to the position that seems so obvious and yet apparently requires re-emphasis:	that if
something is to be done, then we should be told what the principle is upon which that payment is to be made. According to the statement of the government, it is not under the contract.
We now are asked to pass an item of $65 million with no explanation as to the principle which will govern this case or guide members of this house in the future when considering

the application of that principle to other cases. Not only are we told by the Prime Minister that this is not a subject of mathematical calculation; we are told that it is not something that can be calculated in a mathematical manner.
The fact is that the very remarkable statement yesterday of the Minister of Agriculture, which ranged all the way from a political fight in Saskatchewan to a veiled warning to the press that if they did not modify their remarks about him somebody might be haled before the bar of the house, was interlarded with a lot of unrelated figures which in some way that met his satisfaction finally worked out to $65 million. In this case I prefer, and I think members of the house are likely to prefer, to take the statement of the Prime Minister that it is not arrived at by any mathematical process. The Prime Minister has related it to the one figure to which it can properly be related, and that is the balance of the loan that British had coming to them.
That being so, we as elected representatives of the people are being asked to approve a payment of $65 million under no declared principle and under no mathematical calculation. I simply wish to govern the remark I have made by what I said before. I am satisfied that members of this house coming from all parts of Canada are prepared to support any clearly declared and sound principle which will assure that wheat producers, and agricultural producers of any kind, industrial producers or those whose services are required, shall be properly compensated where that production or those services are taken over by compulsion. I have emphasized that at a time when this government has assumed such sweeping emergency powers it is important that some principle be established which will let the people know what they may expect where there is to be compulsion. Nevertheless we have no facts before us from which we can say whether this is too much or too little. It is for that reason that I think hon. members of this house will find it difficult to justify their course if they vote in this particular case.
I come now to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. The hon. member expressed some surprise last night about the position I had taken and seemed to anticipate that I would approve this item. If he had been in the house, or if he was here and had been listening, he would have heard me make it quite clear in the afternoon that I was not prepared to approve the payment of this item, but I said further that I would not support the amendment to reduce the item to one dollar. I gave my reason. The reduction of the item to

It seems to me that an amendment to reduce this item to one dollar implies the acceptance of some unstated principle, and a reduction of the amount given under that principle to what might be regarded as a contemptuous estimate of the value of what is owing under that principle. I am not prepared to support such a proposition, but I am going to vote against this item for the reasons I have given. I suggest to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that this is the proper course. In his case he apparently accepts the principle and then moves to reduce the item to one dollar. I suggest that it is much better to vote straight against the adoption of this item, and that is what I propose to do.

speechtext:
Last night I think the curiosity of the house was aroused by the rather astounding speech of the Minister of Agriculture. I think he sought to leave the impression that, while western farmers were not provided for, eastern Canada farmers had been provided for through subsidies during the war years. He mentioned one item of $169 million for subsidies to the dairy industry. At the outset let me point out that the dairy industry and all other industries at that time were under a ceiling and not a floor, and that the subsidies were given after representations by the dairy industry pointing out that, to maintain production for our own people and

Supply-Agriculture
also to have a highly concentrated nutritious food for our fighting partners in Europe, it was very necessary to pay enough to maintain the high production that the dairy industry established during those years. It bears no relation whatever to the $65 million that we are now discussing.
Actually it seems to me that the payment of the $65 million is an attempt to bail the Minister of Agriculture out of a very embarrassing situation. I should like to mention two agricultural commodities that were dealt with by the minister last night, although there were many others. I have referred to the dairy industry and I want to mention cheese particularly. I know at once that the minister will say that in 1950 the producers asked that cheese be requisitioned. That is true but they did not ask that it be requisitioned at the price that the government set. The government requisitioned it at a lower figure than was suggested by the cheese producers.
As a result of these policies the cheese industry of Ontario is a vanishing one. It was the industry that absorbed a lot of the surplus milk during the summer months. Now we are paying a part of the price of that folly in the ever-increasing price of butter. Incidentally you will note that the price of margarine, the substitute for butter, the cost of which has no relation whatever to the production of butter, has followed the rise in the price of butter. We are paying the price for a policy that was shortsighted so far as the dairy industry was concerned.
It is also interesting to note that in his speech the Minister of Agriculture mentioned three people, the triumvirate, who were going to guide the destinies of this country. I suggest that the Prime Minister has many duties on his hands without trying to steer a course between the divergent views of two ministers, his right and left bowers. I thought it was a rather peculiar statement to make that either of them could make a mistake but the Prime Minister could correct them and get away with it. When eastern members of parliament have talked against the $65 million western producers have said: What about the freight assistance policy? I will tell you about the freight assistance policy. Today the government through the wheat board has the greatest monopoly in the grain trade that ever existed. Whether a monopoly is a government monopoly or otherwise it is a vicious set-up, but above all a government monopoly is certainly the most vicious.
We have reached the point now where a farmer living in western Canada cannot ship grain that he produces to a farm that he owns in eastern Canada. What do we find? The

western producer is getting very little for his feed wheat and coarse grains, and the eastern feeder is paying very high prices for these same products. Somewhere along the way the advantage of the freight assistance policy is being siphoned off. It is not being carried through either to the producer on the one hand or the ultimate consumer on the other.

It certainly was not on the same basis. I am glad the minister says that. It is true that the apple growers in Nova Scotia did receive substantial amounts of money from this government during the war years. Those were payments which the growers appreciated, but those payments were made on a very definite basis, Mr. Chairman. In the first place, it was recognized that the apple industry of Nova Scotia was a war casualty since it was dependent upon markets in Great Britain. The industry was deprived of those markets because of the exigencies of the war. The government intervened to assist the growers. As the minister suggested last night part of the consideration for this assistance, at least for some time, was that we were not allowed to ship apples to the markets of Ontario and Quebec. If we had, Mr. Chairman, the quality of those apples being what it is, undoubtedly we would have wrecked the apple industry of Ontario and Quebec. The demands for assistance which you have heard from the growers in these provinces would have been much more expensive than the cost of the assistance to the fruit industry in Nova Scotia.
The point I want to make is that the fruit industry in Nova Scotia was helped on a mathematical basis. There was no subsidy, but there was a computation of the loss on an accurate basis. I believe the minister will admit that every year representatives of that industry came to Ottawa. They met him and officers of his department as well as officers of the Department of Finance. They presented figures showing the losses they suffered, and in every case they were beaten down. I am not objecting to it, I am simply stating this as a matter of record. The departmental representatives said, "No, you may have taken that loss but the Dominion of Canada cannot assume all of it." They were finally paid on a basis which was a mathematical computation of a proportion of the losses which the fruit industry had suffered, and that is the direct opposite of the policy which is being adopted in this case. This payment is being made on a basis which none of us can compute. Apparently the hon. member for Comox-Alberni arrived at this solution by gazing in a crystal ball and picking out a dollar. We had the Minister of Agriculture suggesting $48 million. Some members suggested $300 million, and some newspapers represented it as $600 million and going up to almost a billion. You are simply told to put your finger in a glass bowl and pay whatever

amount you pull out. It is that principle we protest because it is the reversal of the principle adopted for Nova Scotia.
With respect to the payments made in Nova Scotia I want to point out that a substantial portion of those payments did not go to the growers. They were made for processing apple products which were afterwards distributed by private agencies or by the government, in accordance with government policy, to institutions and to relieve distress throughout the world. I believe that represented a substantial part of the millions to which the minister referred last night.
Those figures also contain moneys being paid for the removal of trees which formerly produced varieties suitable to the British market. Since this market is not now open to us, those trees are being removed or have been removed at a distinct sacrifice to the growers. The amount which the grower has received from this government, helpful though it may have been and appreciated as it is, is only a small part of the actually computed loss which the grower has suffered. I suggest, therefore, there is no validity whatever in using the figures paid to the fruit grower as an illustration of justification of these moneys which are to be paid to the grain producers of western Canada.
I have been confused about this matter, as I am sure other hon. members have been. We would all like to arrive at some basis upon which we could do the right thing, if such a basis can be established. No evidence has been forthcoming as to that.
I am not going to repeat the arguments which have been advanced by my leader and other speakers in this debate. I refer particularly to the statements made by the member for Royal when he reviewed the situation from the standpoint of the maritime farmer. For the reasons which he enumerated I am opposed to this payment at the moment, Mr. Chairman, and I propose to vote against it.
There are other reasons with which I shall deal briefly. We are today in a period of stress and strain for this government. The question of inflation has been before the house on various occasions during this session. What could contribute more to inflation than the payment of millions and millions of dollars at this time without any mathematical basis for it?
The Minister of Finance has been worried about cutting expenditures. He has been worried about extravagance. Undoubtedly he has exercised his influence in attempting to cut expenditures in the various government departments. What are the mail carriers in Vancouver, Regina, Ottawa or Halifax going to say when they walk their route with heavier 80709-00

loads realizing the little saving achieved through their sacrifice, and seeing this $65 million being paid without any basis which is discernible to themselves or anyone else in this country? What will other people say who are called upon to make similar sacrifices when they are confronted with this expenditure which has not been justified in any way?
Mr. Chairman, I hope the member for Comox-Alberni, and our genial friend the member for Temiscouata, who yesterday afternoon tried to quarterback the opposition by suggesting he was prepared to vote for a dollar, will influence the others to join with those of us from this side in expressing our opposition to what we believe is an unjustifiable decision of the government in the light of the information which has been placed before us.

I had no great thought of taking part in this debate until the last few minutes. I would not go so far as to say that hon. members who did not agree with me were talking a lot of nonsense and did not know what they were talking about. I should like to give a man at least credit for his own views, and appreciate that probably he might be as near right as I am myself. I think it is a mistake, and I am sorry that anything has entered into this debate that indicates any hostility toward, or comparison between, subsidies or grants drawn from the east to the west.
I am now talking about agricultural subsidies, and particularly with reference to wheat. I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken that after all agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. That being so, I still think that we must have a prosperous agriculture before we can have a prosperous dominion. I should like to see the western wheat growers and the eastern wheat growers have all the prosperity that they can get.
I want to make a reference to the question that has been raised by the hon. member for Middlesex East. He has mentioned it several times, and again this afternoon he referred to a meeting that he attended in Chatham last year. I attended that meeting myself, and I was one of the delegation that came down here to Ottawa to interview the officials of the Department of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce to see if something could be done to help the situation, because we had a lot of wheat on our hands and no storage, and no place to put it. At

Supply-Agriculture
that time the hon. member for Middlesex East said, and he said it again this afternoon, that there should be some provision made for that under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. I agreed with him. I remember quite distinctly when the prices support act was brought into effect. It was on August 15, 1944, and it made provision for supporting agricultural produce, and the amount was not to exceed $200 million. I was here when that act was brought into effect and became operative. I quite appreciated that it did not take wheat into consideration. Section 2 of the act reads:
(a) "Agricultural product" means any natural product of agriculture (except wheat) designated by the governor in council and includes processed meat, dairy and poultry products, if so designated.
Therefore, under the Agricultural Prices Support Act we have no authority to put a floor price under wheat. I would say to the hon. member that when the Agricultural Prices Support Act comes up for amendment we should try to have it enlarged or made broad enough to embrace Ontario wheat, because it is true that we do not operate under the wheat board. We did at one time, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture well know, and it did not operate very successfully in the east.
When we came to Ottawa and went to the Department of Agriculture-I think the minister was in the west, but his deputy was here-we were told that under the act they had no power to give us any support out of this $200 million. We went to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and he said: "You are not under the wheat board, and we have no authority to purchase your wheat." The only thing that could be done, and it worked out fairly satisfactorily, was to provide storage for the wheat, which they did, and the wheat is now selling at reasonably good prices.
I do want to put something on record that I think should be there. Last night the Minister of Agriculture said that he was carrying around in his pocket the answer to something that was going to be put on the record regarding eastern subsidies, and he had it nearly worn out. I am glad that he had the opportunity to give it. I do not believe that we should go into all the details of it, but I would say this. I received this information from the Department of Finance. It may not be exactly correct, but if it is not correct it is their fault, because they gave it to me. I do want to put on record some of the subsidies that have been paid to the wheat producers and to the wheat farmers of western Canada.

Take the wheat acreage reduction plan. That was a subsidy from 1941 to 1947. It was a policy which induced the people to go out of wheat growing and into the growing of coarse grains and summer fallow. I remember quite well when it was brought up and discussed in the house. It was discussed for some time. From 1941 to 1947 the amount expended on this plan was $86,389,000.

Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to this item of $65 million on the present basis that has been laid before us and I intend to
Supply-Agriculture
vote against it. I should like to put on the record some of the reasons why I am opposed to it and to ask other hon. members if in the light of the information that has been given and of their own statements they too will not agree that this item should not be allowed to pass.
First, I want to say that I agree entirely with what was said by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings with regard to the payment to apple growers being on an entirely different basis from what is being asked here today. I am referring now particularly to the apple growers of British Columbia. They lost their United Kingdom market owing to the shortage of dollars. However, in this case the Minister of Trade and Commerce has assured us that under the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement the wheat growers of Canada secured a larger share of the British market than they had ever had before.
We have asked for justification of this item; we have asked to be told the basis on which the $65 million has been arrived at; but we have not yet been given that information. We have had a large number of completely conflicting statements, not only from ministers of the government who are particularly concerned but from private members on both sides of the house. These statements have been so conflicting as to make it clear that no member, even with the best will in the world and the greatest desire to understand the basis upon which this payment is being asked, could possibly justify support for the payment of $65 million.
At a rough count we have had no fewer than twenty-one different conflicting statements, and I am including the statement made by the hon. member for Peace River just a few minutes ago. The hon. member for Souris, an experienced wheat farmer, estimates the loss at close to $500 million. The Minister of Agriculture stated yesterday he had recommended the holding back on the British loan of $100 million to cover the losses for the first two years of the contract. Yesterday the minister gave five different figures which might be regarded as the total of the losses under the contract. He started with the $100 million, to which I have referred. He then referred to a possible loss of $350 million on one basis of calculation. Another figure was $166 million on another basis, and $118 million on still another basis. Finally we had a figure of $92 million on his fifth proposed basis.
The hon. member for Melfort suggested that the loss was $431 million. The hon. member for Battle River suggested it was

Supply-Agriculture
$568 million. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe suggested that by various computations it might run even as high as $1,000 million. The hon. member for Calgary East suggested that it was $338 million in the first two years. The hon. member for Acadia suggested, that it was $375 million in the first two years. On an earlier occasion the Minister of Agriculture suggested $166 million.
The,hon. member for Assiniboia said it was $555 million. The hon. member for Bow River said it was $568 million. The Minister of Trade and Commerce with most welcome candour said that he did not know just from what point of view the losses could be reckoned. On another occasion the Minister of Agriculture said that he was not sure, and his five different totals would indicate that that is so. He said yesterday, as recorded at page 1475 of Hansard:
It may surprise my hon. friends when they go home at Easter to find out that what I stated here very early in the debate is true, namely, that I have not yet met a single farmer who was asking for 25 cents a bushel-
He went on to say:
-and that I was much nearer right than some of the others are.
The minister does not on this occasion suggest that he is actually right. Then the hon. member for Comox-Alberni suggests that the loss is $1. The hon. member for Leeds shares the same view. He suggests we give $1. The hon. member for Temiscouata suggests that the loss is $1, and said he would be prepared to support an amendment to that effect.

Then the hon. member for Peace River referred this afternoon to the payment of $65 million as a measly, paltry payment of $65 million, only a payment on account.
Finally, to cap the statements, we have the Prime Minister who said that from the start it had been clearly understood that there could not be any mathematical calculation of the consequences of the "have regard to" clause, and $65 million was only a rough approximation of the measure of loss or of expectations, as he put it, of the growers. In addition to the twenty or more conflicting figures which have been given, we have had four different general statements from the ministry as to the basis upon which this r. Fulton.]
money is being requested. Not even the cabinet is agreed on the basis on which this payment should be made. Yet they ask us to approve a huge item of $65 million at a time like this when they themselves can get no closer to agreement on the very basis on which they are asking it.
We start with the Minister of Agriculture who said at first that it was to compensate the farmers because the British had not lived up to their obligations under the agreement. We go from there to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who said that he did not know on what basis the losses could be reckoned, and that in fact the farmers had never been more prosperous than they had under the contract, which had worked to their great advantage. We go from there to the Prime Minister who says that the basis of payment agreed upon by the government is the expectations of certain producer groups. Then we come back to the fourth basis put forward by the Minister of Agriculture yesterday which conflicts even with his earlier statement that it was because of the default of the British.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture said that he could produce figures to show that the payment should be made because of the difference between what the farmers had received and what they would have received if they had obtained world prices for their produce. Of course, Mr. Chairman, it is not surprising that the Minister of Agriculture should make one statement of policy on one occasion and another statement of policy on another occasion. He does not hesitate to differ from his colleagues in the cabinet. Now he has carried it one further logical stage. He does not hesitate to differ from the statement which he made just a week ago in explanation of this request.
I say we need not be surprised at finding this lack of consistent principle, this lack of cabinet solidarity, because the Minister of Agriculture yesterday set forth as his policy that he felt there was no need for consistent statements to be made on different subjects by different ministers, not even the necessity for consistent statements with regard to government policy. At page 1448 of Hansard the Minister of Agriculture stated that that situation should give rise to no wonder, particularly in dealing with the present government, because he said:
One of the reasons why we are satisfied to be where we are-
He was referring to himself and the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
-is that we both know that we can afford to make statements knowing that we might be incorrect...

r"
I wonder if the Minister of Trade and Commerce agrees that he can afford to make statements knowing that he might be incorrect. Nevertheless the Minister of Agriculture, apparently having set that forth as a principle, resents the fact that sometimes it is suggested that his statements are incorrect. I do not know why he should resent that. After all, he says: We know we can afford to make statements even if we know we are incorrect "because we have a leader who does not make many mistakes."
I point out therefore that it is no wonder that we have these conflicting statements before the house as to what is the actual basis of payment. It is no wonder that the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have constantly contradicted each other from the start of this debate. It is no wonder that the Prime Minister had to attempt to reconcile their statements, and the only reconciliation he could effect was to say: Neither of them is correct and the reason we are making the payment is because of the expectations of certain producer groups.
Therefore we have the position that the House of Commons is being asked to vote $65 million without any logical, consistent or coherent explanation of why the taxpayers should be asked to provide that sum of money. We are in a position where we have no basis for this item except the expectations referred to by the Prime Minister. There is a most peculiar thing about these expectations. The Prime Minister indicated that a very large factor contributing to the arousing of these expectations was the statement made by the British food minister. So we are being asked to subscribe to the government policy of payment of $65 million because of a statement of a British minister. I might ask the Prime Minister, I might ask the government, I might ask the Minister of Finance: Since when has the financial or fiscal policy of this government depended upon statements made by British ministers? Since when has the Liberal party reverted to the policy of government from Downing street? The ministers apparently are not prepared to answer, I take it.

In the last statement by a minister as to the basis for this payment the Minister of Agriculture came back to the difference he alleges between what the farmers received and what they would have received at world prices. If that is the basis, whose fault is it that the farmers lost money under the contract? Surely the fault lies with the government whose marketing policy this was. If there be a loss, the basis of which we have not yet been told, that loss is the fault of the government which insisted upon this marketing policy that was attacked in the house by the leader of this party in 1946. The Minister of Agriculture was responsible; yesterday he claimed credit for the marketing policy that has produced this result. If that is the case I can see no other reason for the payment of this money to make up a loss incurred by the farmers under that policy than to retrieve the reputation of the minister, whose lack of qualifications as a dealer in grain has been exposed by the way this contract has worked out.
In 1946 our leader was opposed to this contract. I am therefore opposed to the voting of this money, when we can draw no other conclusion than that the purpose is to redeem the reputation of the Minister of Agriculture.

579. Grants to residential schools-further amount required, $60,668.

I am interested in votes for education. The other day I was pleased to note a vote for education for the town of Rimouski, and I am glad to support a grant for education in any place in the dominion.
I see some money here being given to the Indian schools. When I was speaking on the Indian bill the other day I paid some tribute to the work of those institutions, and I am glad to repeat it. I do want to repeat also that I think that it is best where possible, and particularly for Indian children, that they should, where such schools are available, attend schools in their own districts, whether these schools are run on a denominational or on a public school basis.
My reason of course is simply this, as I said before, that contact can be constantly maintained as between the child and its parents, and that the educational process which goes on in the school can be conveyed daily to the home.


I know the very fine work that these residential schools are doing. I had an opportunity not very long ago to look over one of the residential schools in the constituency of the hon. member for Rosthern. It was the school at Duck Lake. The gentleman who was in charge then-and he was the principal-* said to me-it may be the same man today- that where there was inefficiency in many schools of that type, that inefficiency was due to the lack of money available. He asked me at that time-and I know he has asked other hon. members of parliament-to make a plea so that these residential schools could have the money with which they may proceed to do even better work than they are doing now.
